planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped hollies in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Oakland Holly is a fast-growing hybrid selected for a naturally narrow, dense, oval form that screens effectively in less horizontal space than broader hollies like Nellie R. Stevens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Oakland Holly is a vigorous, fast-growing hybrid holly bred for a naturally narrow, upright, oval form that provides dense, formal screening in a noticeably smaller footprint than broader hollies such as Nellie R. Stevens, making it useful for property-line screens and narrow side yards where space is limited. The glossy, dark green, lightly spined evergreen foliage holds its color and density year-round with minimal pruning required to maintain a neat shape, and the plant produces small red berries in fall and winter that provide food for songbirds. It is heat- and humidity-tolerant, adapts well to Gulf Coast clay soils once established, and shows good resistance to the pests and diseases that can trouble other broadleaf evergreens. Established plants are reasonably drought-tolerant, though regular water during the first one to two years speeds establishment. Prune, if needed, in late winter or after the main flush of new spring growth to maintain the desired screen height and width.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection — Oakland Holly variety notes

North Carolina State Extension — Evergreen Holly Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Steeds is a slow-growing, upright, densely branched Japanese holly cultivar long used as a boxwood substitute in Southern landscapes for its fine texture and tolerance of shearing.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge or screen. Steeds is a classic Japanese holly cultivar valued for its dense, upright, multi-stemmed habit and small, boxwood-like, glossy dark green leaves without the conspicuous spines of many other hollies, making it a popular substitute for boxwood in humid Southern climates where boxwood is prone to blight and decline. It grows slowly into a formal, columnar-to-oval shape that tolerates shearing well, making it a good choice for low hedges, foundation plantings, and formal garden structure, though it also looks attractive left unpruned in its natural upright form. Small black fruit follows inconspicuous flowers, of little ornamental significance compared to red-berried hollies. It tolerates a range of soil conditions but performs best with consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil, and it shows good resistance to the pest and disease pressures that trouble boxwood in the Gulf South. Prune in late winter or after the spring flush if a more formal, sheared shape is desired.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Ilex crenata Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Japanese Holly as a Boxwood Alternative
University of Georgia Extension — Holly Selection Guide

common_name: Eagleston Holly (Southern Hybrid Evergreen Tree Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Eagleston is a fast-growing hybrid tree holly, a cross of American holly and Dahoon holly, long popular as a single-trunk street and specimen tree across the Deep South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing plenty of room for its eventual size as a large tree. Eagleston is a hybrid tree holly (Ilex x attenuata), a cross between American holly (I. opaca) and Dahoon holly (I. cassine), selected for fast growth, a strong single-trunk pyramidal form, and heavy annual crops of bright red berries that persist through winter and feed songbirds. It has been a favorite specimen and street tree across the Deep South for decades, valued for reaching an attractive mature tree form faster than American holly while retaining good foliage density and cold hardiness. The glossy, lightly spined, dark green evergreen leaves provide year-round structure and screening, and the tree tolerates the heat, humidity, and clay soils typical of Gulf South landscapes once established. Like most hollies it is dioecious, so a male holly planted nearby improves berry set, though Eagleston often fruits reasonably well from pollen carried from other hollies in the neighborhood. Prune, if needed, in late winter to maintain a single leader and remove any competing double trunks while the tree is young.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Ilex x attenuata Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Tree Holly Selection
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Hollies for Louisiana Landscapes

common_name: Taylor Juniper (Narrow Columnar Eastern Red Cedar)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Taylor is an extremely narrow, columnar selection of native eastern red cedar discovered in Missouri, useful as a slim vertical accent or narrow screen where a standard red cedar's broader form would not fit.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 4-6 feet apart for a narrow screen or hedge. Taylor is a naturally occurring selection of the native eastern red cedar discovered growing in a Missouri cemetery, prized for an exceptionally narrow, columnar form — often only 3-4 feet wide at maturity despite reaching 15-25 feet tall — that gives it the vertical, formal look of an Italian cypress while retaining the cold hardiness, heat tolerance, and adaptability of native red cedar. The dense, blue-green, scale-like evergreen foliage provides year-round structure, privacy screening, and wildlife cover in a fraction of the horizontal space a standard-form red cedar or arborvitae would require, making it a popular choice for narrow side yards and tight property-line screens. Like other eastern red cedars, it tolerates poor, dry, rocky, or alkaline soils, drought, and heat once established, and needs essentially no supplemental irrigation after the first year or two. Little to no pruning is required to maintain its naturally narrow form; avoid planting in poorly drained sites, since red cedar is prone to root problems in consistently wet soil.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Juniperus virginiana 'Taylor'

common_name: Carolina Sapphire Cypress (Fast-Growing Silvery-Blue Arizona Cypress)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Carolina Sapphire is a fast-growing Arizona cypress selection prized for striking silvery-blue foliage and a citrusy fragrance, but it requires excellent drainage and struggles in heavy, poorly drained Gulf Coast clay.

directions: Plant in full sun in sharply well-drained soil, avoiding heavy clay or any site prone to standing water. Carolina Sapphire is a fast-growing selection of Arizona cypress discovered as a chance seedling in North Carolina, valued for its striking, silvery-blue, finely textured foliage that is among the bluest of any hardy conifer, and for crushed foliage that releases a pleasant citrus-and-mint fragrance. It grows quickly into a dense, broadly pyramidal tree, making it useful as a fast screen or specimen where its color provides strong contrast against green-foliaged evergreens. Unlike the heat- and humidity-tolerant native eastern red cedar, Arizona cypress is adapted to drier climates and is notably intolerant of wet feet, so good drainage is essential; in the heavy clay and high humidity typical of much of the Gulf Coast, root and foliage diseases such as cypress canker and root rot can shorten its lifespan, and it performs best on a raised bed, slope, or sandy, well-drained site. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant and need little supplemental water once roots are established. Prune, if needed, in late winter to maintain shape; avoid overhead irrigation, which increases disease pressure on the foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Carolina Sapphire Cypress introduction and culture
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Arizona Cypress Cultivars
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Conifer Selection for the Southeast
